title: What kind of bug is it?
instruction: Each Python snippet has one bug. Decide when it shows up: Python won’t run the program at all (syntax error), the program crashes while running (runtime error), or it runs but does something different from what it should (logic error).

items.why: The closing quotation mark is missing. Python can’t read the text to the end and won’t even run the program.

items.text: if score > 10   (no colon at the end)   and below it, indented, print("Star!")
items.why: In Python, a condition must be followed by a colon. Without it, it’s an invalid sentence for Python, and nothing runs.

items.text: age = input("How old are you? ")   and then   print(age + 1)
items.why: input returns text, not a number. Python can’t add text and a number, so it crashes when it reaches that line. Fix: int(input(…)).
A list is numbered from zero: 0, 1, 2. Position 3 doesn’t exist, and the program crashes with an IndexError.

items.text: average = points / count   and the player hasn’t played any games yet, so count = 0
items.why: The code itself is fine. The program crashes only for some inputs, here by dividing by zero. That’s why you test with zero too.

items.text: The program should print the numbers 1 to 10:   for i in range(1, 10): print(i)
items.why: range(1, 10) stops before ten. The program runs without an error, it just prints one number too few. The off-by-one error is one of the most common in the world.

items.text: x = 10   and then   while x != 0:   x = x - 3
items.why: Python reports nothing; the program just never stops: x skips over zero (1, −2, −5…). An endless loop is a logic error; the computer does exactly what is written.

items.text: The discount should apply from age 65:   if age > 65: discount = True
items.why: The program runs, but someone who is exactly 65 doesn’t get the discount. A boundary bug, which only a test with the age 65 will expose.

debrief: Python finds a syntax error for you, before you even run the program. It reports a runtime error when it runs into it, and tells you the line number. A logic error can be found by nobody but you and your tests. That’s why tests are written in advance, with boundaries.
